opus-5.5.text:
Teleoperation has been tremendously useful. Most of the recent progress in imitation learning, things like diffusion policies and the large multi-task datasets, rests on people sitting behind a controller and showing the robot what to do. But I think it has some fundamental limitations, and I usually group them into three.

The first is scale. Teleoperation is expensive. You need the physical robot, a trained operator, and someone to reset the scene, and you collect data at roughly real-time speed, often slower, because operating a robot through a VR headset or a puppet arm is harder than just doing the task with your hands. Compare that to language or vision models trained on internet-scale data. We're talking about orders of magnitude less data, and teleoperation alone isn't going to close that gap. It grows linearly with human labor and robot hours.

The second is quality and naturalness. When people teleoperate, they don't behave the way they would if they did the task themselves. Latency, limited haptic feedback, and the mismatch between the human body and the robot all make the demonstrations slow, hesitant, and sometimes inconsistent. They're also usually biased toward success. Operators recover from mistakes in idiosyncratic ways, and the data rarely covers the failure states the policy will actually drift into at deployment. So you get the classic distribution shift problem.

The third is that the data is tied to the embodiment. A dataset collected on one robot arm with one gripper and one camera setup doesn't transfer cleanly to another. You end up re-collecting for every new platform, which makes the scaling problem even worse.

That's why a lot of my group's thinking has moved toward other data sources. We're looking at human data, like people doing tasks naturally while wearing egocentric sensors such as cameras or AR glasses. That data is much cheaper, much more diverse, and captures how humans actually manipulate things. The challenge is the embodiment gap between human hands and robot hands, so the research question becomes how to learn representations and policies that bridge humans and robots. Simulation and generated data play a role too.

So I don't think teleoperation goes away. It's very good for grounding and fine-tuning on the actual robot. But I think of it as the high-quality, low-quantity part of the data pyramid, not the foundation. The foundation has to come from somewhere more scalable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think about this a lot, because teleoperation has really been the workhorse of the whole imitation learning wave over the last few years, and for good reason. It's the most direct way to get data that is actually in the robot's own action space. You put a person behind a VR controller or a leader arm, they do the task, and you get observations paired with motor commands. That's exactly what a policy needs.

But there are a few limitations that I think people underappreciate.

The first one is just the economics. Teleop scales linearly with human time. Every hour of robot data costs roughly an hour of a person's attention, plus setup, plus resets, plus the failures you throw away. Compare that to language models, where the data was already sitting there as a byproduct of people living their lives. Nobody wrote the internet to train GPT. With teleop, we are deliberately manufacturing every single sample, and there is no obvious flywheel that makes the next hour cheaper than the last.

The second limitation is more subtle, and it's about what the data actually contains. Teleop data captures what a human does when they're driving a robot through a particular interface. That's not the same thing as what a human does with their own body, and it's not the same as what the robot should do. The interface imposes its own biases. People move slower, they're more conservative, they avoid contact-rich strategies because they can't feel anything. So you end up learning a kind of strange hybrid behavior, the ergonomics of the teleop setup encoded into the policy. And the demonstrations are also really low in diversity in ways that matter. Human operators tend to be consistent. They'll grasp the mug the same way fifty times. That's good for cloning, but it means the policy has seen very little of the state space near the demonstrations, and when it drifts off, it has no idea how to recover.

Which brings me to the third thing, which is that teleop data has almost no information about failure and recovery. The operator usually succeeds, or you discard the episode. But a robot in the real world is going to make small mistakes constantly, and the thing that separates a usable system from a demo is whether it can notice and fix those mistakes. Pure demonstration data basically doesn't teach that. You can try to patch it with DAgger-style corrections or with human-in-the-loop intervention, and those help, but then you're back to the first problem, you're spending even more human time per useful unit of information.

And then the last thing I'd say is that teleop data is tied to a specific embodiment. You collect on one arm, one gripper, one camera placement, and the data is only partially transferable. Cross-embodiment work has made some progress there, but it's still much harder than, say, moving a language dataset between model architectures.

So my view is not that teleop is bad. It's that teleop is the bootstrapping mechanism, not the end state. It gets you a policy that is competent enough to start generating its own experience. The interesting question is what happens after that. How do you let robots improve from their own rollouts, from simulation, from human video, from forms of supervision that aren't someone holding a controller. That's where I think the field has to go if we want robots that actually scale, rather than robots that scale as fast as we can hire operators.

astra-6.text:
I think teleoperation is a really useful way to collect demonstrations, but we have to distinguish between showing a robot how to succeed and giving it enough experience to handle everything that can go wrong.

With teleoperation, a person is closing the loop. They see something slipping, adjust the grasp, and compensate for mistakes. The robot gets a record of those actions, but learning the underlying reasons for those corrections is much harder. And when you deploy the learned policy, it may reach situations that weren’t represented in the demonstrations. It needs to know how to recover, not just how to repeat a successful trajectory.

There’s also a coverage problem. Collecting more demonstrations takes human time, and adding more hours doesn’t necessarily give you the diversity you need across objects, environments, and failures. The interface itself can also limit what people demonstrate, especially for tasks requiring fast reactions or subtle force feedback.

So I see teleoperation as a valuable starting point. It gives the robot a useful prior for what to do. But I think we also need ways for robots to learn from their own interaction and failures, rather than relying entirely on people to demonstrate every possible situation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think teleoperation is a very useful way to get robots started, but it has a few fundamental limitations. One is scale: you need a person operating a robot to collect each demonstration, and that takes time and effort. If you want to cover lots of tasks, environments, and objects, that becomes expensive.

Another limitation is the distribution of the data. A skilled operator tends to demonstrate successful behavior. But once you deploy a learned policy, the robot makes mistakes and ends up in states that weren’t in those demonstrations. The data may tell it how to do the task when everything goes well, without teaching it how to recover when something goes wrong.

And teleoperation is itself an interface. What the operator can perceive, and how easily they can control the robot, affects the behaviors you collect. So I see it as an important starting point, but we also need ways for robots to learn from their own experience, including failures, rather than depending entirely on more human demonstrations.
